name: ccextractor
desc: Tool for extracting closed captions from video files
why: Pulls hidden closed-caption data out of video streams, a window into how captions are smuggled inside broadcast bitstreams.

brief.what_it_is: CCExtractor is an open source command-line tool (with a Windows GUI and a Flutter GUI) that extracts closed captions and subtitles from TV recordings and other media files. You give it an input file, such as a .ts transport stream, and it writes subtitle output, with SRT and WebVTT among the formats the README mentions. The README also lists real-time extraction, translating subtitles, extracting closed captions from DVDs, and converting closed captions to subtitles. The core is written in C, with some C++ and Python and optional Rust components.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says subtitles matter to many people: language learners, and people who are hard of hearing. The project's stated aim is to make subtitle generation easy from the command line or a Windows GUI, and to keep up with all broadcast sources and formats around the world. The homepage adds that its .srt output is used by millions, since many externally downloaded TV subtitle files originally came from it.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internal mechanism for pulling caption data out of video streams. It only says that running ccextractor on an input extracts the subtitles, and that running it with no arguments lists its parameters. It does say that WebVTT output can optionally include an X-TIMESTAMP-MAP header, which HLS workflows need.

brief.install_notes: Precompiled binaries and source are on the project website downloads page. Windows users can use WinGet, Chocolatey, or Scoop, and Scoop needs the extras bucket added first. Building from source on Linux uses autotools in the linux/ directory: cd linux, ./autogen.sh, ./configure, make. Rust support is switched on automatically if cargo and rustc are present, and the README recommends make clean or a fresh clone if builds or links go wrong, especially with Rust involved. Windows builds can go through WSL, with instructions in docs/build-wsl.md. The full compilation guide is docs/COMPILATION.MD. No accounts or runtime setup are mentioned.
brief.standout: The homepage claims that its .srt output is the de facto standard, even though the software is niche and its users are mainly universities, media companies, and enthusiasts. The README does not discuss hidden caption data inside broadcast bitstreams, so that framing comes from the editor's scout note rather than from the project.
brief.status: Maintained, with partial evidence. The README shows live Sample-Platform build-status badges for Windows and Linux, plus download counters on SourceForge and GitHub. The homepage is labelled as still in beta and asks for GSoC'26 applicants, so development is active. I did not see a release date or last-commit date, so the exact recency is unknown.
brief.caveats: The homepage says it is still in beta and may have formatting errors or missing pages. The organization is informal and not incorporated, and volunteers coordinate it. The README's Linux build notes say the autotools path has been tested only on Linux and WSL, and that unexpected build or link problems are likely, especially with Rust. Licensed under GPL-2.0. The README refers to a Slack channel and an email address for support, but the homepage points to a Zulip instance, so the chat platform the project actually uses is unclear.
